Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-2-prompt-long-0128", "row_sha256": "d2c6041464569a0015858b4195e1e6413803899182fccbc1af4cd315ddaa8fec", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "i'm trying to get a clear request together for the photo catalogue work. please make a proposed index for the family photo catalogue, but only if the date or date range written on every one of the 14 scanned album indexes can be supported by either a postmarked envelope kept with that album or two independent dated family notes that identify the album or the event. the evidence has to support the written year or range, not just show that somebody owned the album at some point. if even one album doesn't meet that test, don't make the proposed index; instead make a date-review list of the albums that fail it. that alternate list is actually useful because we've been putting off checking a handful of labels, and it shouldn't turn into a reorganization of the whole catalogue.

the catalogue covers family photographs from 1968 through 2004. right now it is made up of 14 scanned album indexes plus six folders of loose photographs. for the main action, use the album indexes only: take the existing entries and propose arranging them first by year and then by event where an event is recorded. keep each album and its page references attached to the entry so we can trace it back to the scan. this is a proposal, not permission to rename albums, change scans, or move anything in the catalogue. the loose-photo folders are outside this indexing task, even if a folder seems to fill a gap in an album's dates.

1. material and fields to use. the scans have a mix of album titles, handwritten dates or date ranges, page numbers, captions for events or places, and scan filenames. use a field only where the index actually has it. several entries have no event caption, some page numbers are hard to read, and a few filenames have only a short label like `album_07a`. keep those gaps as gaps instead of guessing. the red cloth album has a title page and a few numbered sections; the blue linen album has dates written on the inside cover; and the narrow black album is scanned as two files even though it is one album. don't turn the two files into separate albums. the catalogue already has an entry for each of these, so the task is to work from those entries rather than create new records.

the notes and envelopes are not arranged neatly. there are envelopes in a box marked “Mum's papers,” notes copied into the back of a small address book, and a few loose cards filed beside the scans. a postmark may be useful only when it can be connected to the album in question and supports its stated date. likewise, the two notes have to be independent of each other; two copies of the same note don't count. a note that names a person but not an album or event may not identify the relevant photographs. one note says, “the lake weekend after Nora started school,” but that wording by itself doesn't give a year. don't silently convert a seasonal memory or a person's age into a date.

some of the handwriting is hard to read, and the materials don't all use the same date style. one index says `summer 1981`, another has `1981–83`, and a few have only a year with a question mark. there are also entries where a pencilled correction sits beside the first date. please keep the original written date visible in whichever deliverable applies, and distinguish it from any evidence you use to assess it. don't resolve a disagreement just by choosing the neater-looking date. the point of the condition is to decide whether each album's recorded date or range has adequate support, not to settle every family-history question.

if every one of the 14 album dates passes the condition, make the proposed index with year as the first grouping and recorded events as the next grouping where available. preserve the album title, relevant page references, recorded caption and scan filename when present, and keep an album together if its index spans more than one year. if the recorded range crosses years, show the range rather than silently assigning the album to a single year. if the condition is not met, make the different, narrower date-review list instead: include only albums whose dates fail the test, with the title as recorded, its date or range as written, and a brief indication of what evidence is present or missing. don't include albums that pass in that fallback list.

there are two old working aids in the box, a handwritten event list and a photocopy of an index from before the scans were made. they may help connect a note or envelope to an album, but they are not a substitute for the stated evidence test and they are not new catalogue entries. filenames can help identify which scan is which; they don't establish a date. please treat the materials as uneven rather than assuming every album has the same amount of documentation.

return only the one deliverable selected by the condition: either the proposed index or the date-review list. no introduction, explanation of your process, or second version. don't edit the scanned images, infer identities for unnamed people, or add events that aren't in the existing index. the purpose is to make the catalogue easier for the family to consult while leaving the underlying scans and their recorded information untouched.", "output": "Please prepare one deliverable for the family photo catalogue, based on the condition below. Do not edit or rename the scans, alter catalogue records, or reorganize the loose-photo folders.

The catalogue covers photographs from 1968 through 2004. It contains 14 scanned album indexes and six folders of loose photographs. Work from the 14 album-index entries only. Use the existing titles, handwritten dates or date ranges, page references, event or place captions, and scan filenames wherever they are present. Leave absent or unreadable information blank rather than guessing. The red cloth album has a title page and numbered sections; the blue linen album has dates on its inside cover; and the narrow black album appears in two scan files but is one album. Keep the black album as one record, and do not create new catalogue entries.

To assess the condition, use the available postmarked envelopes and dated family notes. A postmarked envelope counts only if it can be connected to the album and supports its recorded year or date range. Alternatively, the date or range must be supported by two independent dated family notes that identify the album or event. Two copies of one note are not independent. Evidence that only shows ownership, names a person without identifying the album or event, or gives an undated memory does not establish the album’s date. For example, the note “the lake weekend after Nora started school” does not by itself supply a year. Do not infer dates from seasons, ages, or other clues.

Some date entries have uncertain handwriting, different formats, or pencilled corrections. Examples include `summer 1981`, `1981–83`, and a year followed by a question mark. Keep each album’s original written date visible and distinguish it from the supporting evidence. Do not choose between conflicting dates merely because one looks clearer. The test is whether each recorded date or range has adequate support, not whether every family-history question can be settled.

1. **If every one of the 14 albums meets the evidence test:** prepare a proposed index grouped first by year and then by recorded event where available. Keep each album and its page references traceable to its scan. Include the recorded title, relevant page references, caption, and scan filename when present. Keep an album together when its index spans more than one year, and show a recorded range as a range rather than assigning it to one year.

2. **If any album fails the test:** do not prepare the proposed index. Instead, prepare a date-review list containing only the albums that fail. For each, give the title as recorded, the date or range as written, and a brief indication of what relevant evidence is present or missing. Do not include albums that pass in this list.

The envelopes and notes are stored in several places: a box marked “Mum's papers,” the back of a small address book, and loose cards filed beside the scans. The handwritten event list and photocopied pre-scan index may help connect an item of evidence to an album, but they do not replace the evidence test and are not new catalogue entries. A filename may identify a scan but does not establish a date. Treat the documentation as uneven; do not assume every album has the same supporting material.

Return only the single deliverable selected by the condition: either the proposed index or the date-review list. Do not add an introduction, process explanation, or second version. Do not infer identities for unnamed people or add events absent from the existing index. The task is to make the catalogue easier for the family to consult while leaving the scans and their recorded information untouched."}]
